title: Software agent
summary:
In computer science, a software agent is a computer program that acts for a user or another program in a relationship of agency. The term agent is derived from the Latin agere (to do): an agreement to act on ones behalf. Such action on behalf of implies the authority to decide which, if any, action is appropriate. Some agents are colloquially known as bots, from robot.

They may be embodied, as when execution is paired with a robot body, or as software such as a chatbot executing on a computer. Software agents may be autonomous or work together with other agents or people. Software agents interacting with people may possess human-like qualities such as natural language understanding and speech, personality, or embody humanoid form.

Related and derived concepts include intelligent agents, autonomous agents (capable of modifying the methods of achieving their objectives), distributed agents, multi-agent systems, and mobile agents (agents that can relocate their execution onto different processors). The concept of an agent can be traced back to Hewitts Actor Model (1977), described as a self-contained, interactive and concurrently-executing object, possessing internal state and communication capability.

Software agent systems are a direct evolution of Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), which evolved from Distributed Artificial Intelligence (DAI), Distributed Problem Solving (DPS) and Parallel AI (PAI). The cultural effects of software agents include trust affliction, skills erosion, privacy attrition and social detachment. Those who start relying solely on intelligent agents may lose important skills relating to information literacy.
